t: Shortest Uncommon Substring in an Array
o: For each string, find its shortest substring appearing in no other string, breaking ties lexicographically; output "" if none exists. In ["cab","ad","bad","c"], "cab" yields "ab" (shortest, lex-smallest among "ab"/"ca"), "ad" and "c" yield "". With n ≤ 100 and lengths ≤ 20, each string has at most 210 substrings, so generating all substrings and counting how many strings contain each is at most ~21,000 substring insertions — trivially fast. The main care points are deduplicating substrings within one string (so counting uses distinct substrings per string) and the tie-breaking order.
k: Each string contributes at most L(L+1)/2 ≤ 210 distinct substrings, so exhaustive enumeration is cheap.
Count, for each substring, the number of strings containing it; a substring is 'uncommon' for string i iff its count is 1 and it comes from i.
Scan candidates by (length, lexicographic) order to satisfy both tie-breaks.

a.n: Approach 1: Hash map of substring counts
a.i: Collect the set of substrings of every string, increment a global counter per distinct substring per string, then for each string pick the shortest (lex-smallest) substring whose global count is 1.
s: For each string, build the set of all its substrings and increment counters.
For each string, scan its substrings with count == 1.
Track the best by length then lexicographic order; default to "".
a.t: O(n · L³) with tiny constants — about 100 · 20³ = 800k character operations.

a.i: Insert every substring of every string into a trie, incrementing a node's counter only the first time a given string reaches it (dedupe per string via a visited set). A node with count 1 marks a substring unique to one string; walking each candidate substring through the trie reads its count in O(length).
s: Build a trie; for each string, insert all its substrings, counting each distinct node once per string.
For each string, enumerate its substrings, walk the trie, and record candidates whose terminal count is 1.
Pick the shortest, lex-smallest candidate per string.
a.t: O(n · L³) — same asymptotics as hashing, with trie nodes shared across common prefixes.
a.sp: O(n · L³) trie nodes in the worst case.

w: The hash-map solution is the pragmatic interview choice; mention the trie to show structure awareness (it wins when memory sharing matters or queries arrive online). Critical pitfall: counting a substring once per string, not once per occurrence, otherwise duplicated substrings inside one string inflate counts. Also remember the empty-string fallback. Follow-up: stream the strings and answer per-string queries as they arrive, or find the shortest substring unique to at least k strings.
